utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. Case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber has four oral decisions to render, three in open session, one in private session, and then I will turn to Mr. Praljak. First decision with regard to the admission into evidence of exhibits in relation to Witness BX who appeared on 25th of October, 2006. The Chamber will now be stating its position with regard to the admissibility of exhibits concerning Witness BX. The Chamber will admit the following exhibits presented by the Prosecution since they have certain probative value and certain relevance: P 09710 under seal will be admitted. P 01371. In addition, the Chamber decides to admit 3D 00474 presented by the Defence representing Mr. Praljak, since this exhibit has both probative value and relevance. Second oral decision concerning admission into evidence of documents concerning Witness BV. The Chamber will state its position with regard to the admission into evidence of these exhibits of the witness who appeared on the 18th and 19th of October. The Chamber will admit the following exhibits presented by the Prosecution since they have both a certain probative value and certain relevance. P 01326, P 01371, P 01413, P 01636, P 09146, P 09724 under seal. In addition, the Chamber will admit the following exhibits presented by the Defence given that they have certain probative value and relevance: 3D 00467 under seal. The Chamber, however, will not admit an exhibit presented by the Defence for Praljak, Mr. Praljak, the number of which hasn't yet been disclosed to the Chamber since it hasn't been filed. It hasn't been registered in the Ringtail database. Third decision concerning the joint motion of the Defence for the Prosecution to complete the chart of the 4th of September required by the order of the 3rd of November, 2005. In the motion dated the 2nd of October, 2006, the Defence asked the Chamber to order the Prosecution to complete the list of exhibits and witnesses filed on the 4th of October, 2006, in accordance with the order dated the 30th of November, 2005. The Prosecution responded and provided various reasons to justify the fact that certain information was missing. At the pre-trial stage, after the preliminary motions had been dealt with, the Pre-Trial Judge asked the Prosecution to present 65 ter lists of witnesses and exhibits in a chart. The chart was not supposed to add information in the indictment since this issue had already been dealt with. It was a matter of establishing a link between witnesses and the exhibits and precise information concerning the charges and responsibility of the accused in the amended indictment. The Chamber familiarised itself with the chart of the 4th of September, 2006, and would like to note that the Prosecution has taken certain steps and mentioned or has referred to most of the information that was missing and was required. Naturally, the chart could have been more complete, and one could have included the dates and the perpetrators or groups of perpetrators involved in the events referred to in the indictment. However, at this stage of the proceedings the Chamber believes that it is not necessary for the Prosecution to provide more ample information regarding the chart, given the fact that one is aware of the burden of work they have. However, the Chamber invites the Prosecution, when making its case, to emphasise certain aspects in the indictment. For example, when witnesses are called to testify with regard to Count 1 in the indictment, crime of prosecution -- of persecution, the Prosecution must use these witnesses and the exhibits used to underline which perpetrators are concerned and to underline the dates concerned. As a result, the Chamber rejects the joint motion of the Defence and invites the Prosecution to show due diligence when making its case by identifying the charges, the events that have been alleged in the indictment more precisely. And I would just like to note something myself. When witnesses appear, the Chamber would like the Prosecution to ensure that the witnesses state who the perpetrators of the crimes are, if that is possible, and to specify the dates. If the Prosecution isn't in a position to do this, the Chamber will do this. Decision, oral decision number four, but now we will open into open -- into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, did there come a time in January 1993 that the village of Dusa was attacked by shells?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you remember the date when -- when Dusa was shelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't remember the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you know who shelled the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. The HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how do you know it was the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we knew. We were already in the basement, so guards had been set up. It couldn't have been anyone else.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak up a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Maybe we could have both microphones on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, you will have to move a bit closer to the microphone because the interpreters have a difficulty hearing you. Did this attack came as a surprise to you and the other villagers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, because we really didn't think they would attack us as there were these joint guards. We didn't really believe there would be such a conflict between the Croats and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now you've said before that you know it was the HVO because "we were already in the basement and guards had been set up." Does that mean that before the attack took place there was already indications that -- that something was going to happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. There was this first clash in June 1992, the first clash with the Croats, and then they parted ways. They no longer had these joint guards. The armija had its own guards, and the Croats had their own guards. That was the first clash in 1992. The attack lasted for an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But, Witness, what I was actually referring to is -- is again January 1993. You said that your village was shelled but that already in the days before there were indications that something was going to happen, and I would like you to ask -- to say a bit more about that period of time. So just prior to the -- to the shelling. Let me just ask you, when was it first became apparent to you and the other villagers that -- that something was going to happen in -- in the region in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The army knew, but they didn't want to talk about it in detail. They didn't want to frighten us and tell us that something was expected to happen in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When you say "the army," which army are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the army that had organised itself in Dusa, the guards that were there and were observing what was being done on the other side. They said that the HVO was digging in, that they were bringing in heavy weapons, and that they noticed that there would be a conflict between the armija and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Talking about the army that organised itself in Dusa, who were these men? Were these local men or also people from outside Dusa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They were local men. It was a small village. There can't have been more man 20 men because there were quite a few elderly people in Uzricje, Dusa, that was one area. They linked up, from Uzricje to Dusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did they have weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They only had rifles. They didn't have any heavy weapons. They didn't even have much ammunition. They had these rifles and they only had some bullets. They had nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, you said that the local men from Dusa were saying that -- observing that the HVO was digging in and that they were bringing in heavy weapons. Did you yourself see any -- any of that, that the HVO was bringing in heavy weapons or was preparing for some sort of attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't personally see that. When groups arrived or they talk about these things that I as a woman didn't see this, but there were the troops that were there, and they'd talk about these things. These were people who saw what was happening. They saw things being brought in. But we had been encircled. We couldn't get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So you're saying you've been -- you were encircled. Now, could you yourself see that you were encircled?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Excuse me, Your Honour. The question as it's being posed at this point is assuming a fact that's not in evidence. I don't believe she said --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, she said herself --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. Let me make my record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, don't interrupt the pace. As I said a while ago, we want to know who did what, who was there. This is what will be referred to in the Judgement. We're wasting time. We have to go to the crux of the matter. We need to know the following: She said there were heavy weapons. The Prosecutor asked her whether she had seen these heavy weapons. She said no. So it's hearsay. And now we have to move on. If you break the pace for procedural reasons, I'm going to have to put the question to the witness myself, and the situation will be identical when you call your own witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's not a procedure. He's paraphrasing what he believes the witness stated. I'm not trying to break the flow. She said she didn't observe. I think we need to take it step by step, and he should not be assuming a fact that's not in evidence. That's my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You're quite right about that point. Mr. Bos, please put brief questions to the witness so that we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, how -- how did you and the other civilians react to what was happening in the region at the time? You said that the men were preparing a defence. What -- what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were sitting in the basement. We were afraid. We saw that there was no way out because the defence wasn't sufficiently good for them to be able to defend themselves. We were just waiting to see what would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, you're saying, "We were sitting in the basement." Who are you referring to? Was that just you or were there other civilians in the basement as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the civilians were sitting there in the basement. Those who had livestock would go out in the night to feed them and then they'd return to sleep in the basement. And as I said, we were waiting to see what would happen, and the worst happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And when you say "all of the civilians," can you give a number? How many people are we talking about then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were about 65 of them. I didn't count them, but perhaps there were even more of them. There were some in another house, too, so perhaps there were even more of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You said, "We were waiting to see what would happen, and the worst happened." Now, I would like to talk to you about -- about -- about that. What happened on -- on the day of the shelling? And maybe just describe from the start. What -- of what your experiences on that day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, Mr. Karnavas could have stood up; he hasn't done so. But she said, "We were expecting the worst." You said, "What about shelling?" You could have asked her, "What is the worst?" She would then have said, "It's shelling." That's how we could have proceeded. We'll deal with this question after the break. It's now 10.35. We'll have a 20-minute break and we will resume at about 11.00 -- about five to 11.00. Madam, during the break you can make a sketch of your house on a piece of paper, and to the extent that it's possible you should mark the level at which the basement was, the first floor, the second floor. We will resume at five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, please try and move on more rapidly, because we are short of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, you were asked to make a drawing of your -- a sketch of the house. I see you've drawn up a sketch.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could we please put that on the ELMO so that everyone can see the sketch.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you just explain because there's a couple of words written probably in B/C/S. What does the word "podrum" mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The word "podrum" means the basement. That was where we had taken shelter. And then above we have the first floor, and then we have the balcony which stretched from one side of the house to the other. The balcony and terrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What we see here is the front of the house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If we can move on, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could you put your initials on the piece of paper. Mr. Bos, you would like this document to be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... be given an IC number and I think it will be IC 67.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And, Witness, maybe you could just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar IC 67 under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: IC 67 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Maybe you could put your initials and the date in the right-hand corner of the sketch.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: 27 October. Initials, or name. It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If we could put this under seal, Your Honour. That's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, before the break you said that the worst happened to you. Where were you when the worst happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And who was with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the other civilians were with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you describe in your own words what happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The night was very calm, very quiet. In the morning the situation was the same. It was quiet. You couldn't hear any shots being fired, but people were still afraid because it was so quiet. We talked about certain things, wondered whether something was being prepared. Everyone was afraid. No one told us anything about what was going on. They couldn't leave the lines to tell us about the situation. In the morning I went up to the floor to fetch something. Quite by chance I looked out of the window from the balcony and across the road you could see two tanks that had taken up position. I returned immediately. I was afraid. I returned to the basement. I told them what I had seen. And I didn't leave the basement again because I was scared. So I didn't leave the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Then what happened? Please continue to describe what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, I'm afraid I've forgotten the exact time. It was all so shocking. It was very quiet before that, so I don't know exactly when it was that shells started falling. We started counting them, one, two, three, four, and one hit the basement. And then there was chaos, wounding. The civilians who were not wounded --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you there. You say then a shell hit the basement. What -- what happened to you when the shell hit the basement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was wounded, and I don't remember after that. When I regained consciousness, I know that the basement was full of people, so I can't remember exactly what happened to the others, where the civilians were. There was a man crying. His wife had been killed. His daughter was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there again. You said you were wounded. Can you describe to the Court what kind of wounds you obtained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I was wounded in the head and the jaw. Two teeth were broken and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Take your time, Witness. Maybe just take a little bit of water. Witness, you said that you saw a man who was crying. Do you know the name of this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Abid Behlo, who was crying, he was carrying his wife and child. I tried getting up to see whether it was my children, but he said, "No, it's my wife and daughter." Then I went to the other corner of the basement and there was a girl in a very serious condition lying there, and her father, Ceho Salih, was also badly wounded. They were asking for water. His daughter was asking for water, for me to give her some. And then our soldiers heard the screams. They withdrew from the lines and they came to help, to help the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me just stop you there. Just to go back a bit, you've identified the person who was crying as Abid Behlo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You said that he was carrying his wife and child. The name of this -- of this wife and child?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sabaha and Mirsada. And his son was killed, Mirsad, about 20 metres away from the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Was this Abid Behlo and -- were they inhabitants of Upper Dusa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They were from Paloc. They were in the Croatian part. And during the night they were afraid, and they came and joined us in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, you said, "Our soldiers heard the screams and they withdrew from the lines and came to help the civilians." Let me just ask you a question. So at the time these shells were hitting the house, were any of the men or the soldiers in the house at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There wasn't a single soldier there, only the older people and the wounded. There may have been four or five old men, but not a single soldier in the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So what happened when they withdrew the lines and came to help?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came to save us, to see who was wounded, to help them, because we didn't have any first aid bandages. Then they found something in the house, some white sheets which they tore up, and they extended aid and bandaged all of us, and then they stayed for a while. I don't know how long. Then they removed the dead bodies. They put them in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, you've been referring to dead bodies. Do you know the persons who got killed on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, of course. I told you Sabaha Behlo; her daughter Mirsada; son Mirsad; Fatka Gudic; Enisa Behlo, who was pregnant, two or three months pregnant; Muamer Zulum who died there, he was a 14-year-old boy; Salih Ceho who died in hospital from the wounds he suffered.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, you've given us several names. What I'd like to do now is go name by name, and if you could then -- and some of them we've already discussed, but could you tell -- I will ask -- give you the name, and could you tell me how you -- to your knowledge, how that person got killed. And maybe first start with Sabaha Behlo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How she lost her life?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was unconscious, so I didn't know that actually what happened that very moment. I just know that she was killed by a shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And was she killed in the basement or outside the basement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She was killed just in front of the basement. However, Sabaha and Mirsada were killed in the basement, because when the shell fell, she was shot. And Fatka Gudic and Muamer and Zulum and the others were killed as they started running towards Smailo's house. This was a new house built in 1992, and that is where Sabaha was killed. And Salih, Mirsad, Muamer, as they were running away, as the shells were falling on the house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, it's a bit confusing for us. Could you please make a clear distinction between those who were killed while they were in the basement. So give us the names of those who were killed at the same time that you were wounded and rendered unconscious, and those who were killed outside the basement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the basement people were only seriously wounded. But when Sabaha and her daughter starting running, they were killed at the door because the shells were falling. However, when the shell fell at the -- in the basement itself, people were badly wounded, and they panicked and they started running away, and Sabaha and her daughter were killed on the way out, because another shell fell there. And the others were killed as shells continued falling on Smailo's house. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Shells -- you say shells were falling. Did you have a conception of where the shell came from? Did they come from the sky, fall down, or did they come more or less horizontally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think they were falling from Mackovac, Kupres. That's the only way that the shells could reach our houses. It was only from that direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But when a shell strikes and when it caused loss of consciousness, did it pass through the roof and hit the basement, or did it come from the side? Could you explain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It -- I think I draw a little -- I drew a little circle on the house. It struck the house through the wall, left the big hole and entered the basement. It was aimed at the basement. It didn't come through the roof. Anyone could see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Because this is important for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness BY, a point of clarification. Within the general framework of what you're telling us, you said that when you were hit the men who were outside, in order to protect the village, heard the cries and came to join you, which means that they weren't very far away. I would like to appeal to your feeling of responsibility, because you know the Chamber is seeking to establish the truth. Could you say that actually there was an exchange of fire between the men who were not far from the basement and the forces that you saw from your window near the village? Could one say that there was an exchange of fire at a certain point in time before the basement was hit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And let me add to this question, which is of special importance for us, asking you to tell us about the men who were protecting you. How far were they from your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't very far, because they couldn't go far because we were encircled on all sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How far? 10 metres, 50 metres, a hundred metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe 200 metres, not more than that. Maybe even a hundred metres. I'm afraid I can't tell you with accuracy. But it wasn't far. You could go out and see them, if you had been free to move around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're telling us about a hundred metres. Now, my learned friend has asked you whether the men who were protecting the village had opened fire at those who were shelling.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How can he do anything with a rifle? They didn't have any heavy weapons. We all know what a rifle can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not the question, madam. The question is to see whether the men had opened fire, even with a rifle. 13

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't tell you. I wasn't there with them. You can hear the bullets, but you don't know where the shots are coming from. It's only when the shells fell that we knew. So I really can't tell you whether they fired or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're just telling us you could hear the sound of the bullets, but you didn't know where they were coming from. But before the shell pierced the wall, did you hear the bullet shots?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This was afterwards when we left the basement. You could hear the whistle of the bullets because we were told not to walk around the village to avoid being wounded again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Afterwards, but not before the shell hit your house. Not before. Before that you didn't hear bullet shots.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, a moment ago you said you thought the shells about falling from Kupres and Mackovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit 91 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not Kupres. I didn't say Kupres. I said Mracaj -- Mackovac. It's quite a different location.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. Could the witness be shown Exhibit 9146, photograph number 6, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, can you indicate on this photograph where you think that the shells were coming from, and maybe mark that with an X.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, while she's looking at, I think we need to make a redaction on page 39, line 4. I think the word "your" may have to be redacted here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. Witness, I see you've marked an X on where you thought that the shells were coming from. Now, about 10 minutes ago you also told the Court that on the morning of this day you went out and you saw two tanks. Can you indicate on this particular photograph --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: -- where you -- where you saw these two tanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Maybe where you've marked this X, maybe you can put the word -- put the word "tank." Can you write the word "tank" near that mark.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should write it down?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, please write down "tank."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can we get an IC number for this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: While it is still on, may I ask. It appears that where the crosses for the tanks are there is a forest. Is that correct? Were they in the woods on the other side of the valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a road there and they were on the road. There was no forest in our direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, just to follow up on this question, where did that road lead to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Towards Prozor, Pidris.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, again could you maybe put your initials and the date of today, 27 October, on the corner of this -- of this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And if I could get an IC number for this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That will be Exhibit IC 68, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, you referred to photographs. When going through the photographs, it seems that 275 --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- could testify about this -- this famous road.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes. If Your Honours wish so, we can -- if we can get Exhibit 9146 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because for the Judges, we have to know whether the tank was hidden in the forest, and then the witness can't see the tank, or is the tank on the road and can it be seen from the window. There is a photograph that might be able to help us resolve this difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I agree, and -- so I'll ask the witness to be shown Exhibit 9146, photograph number, and I will have to count now. Photograph number 12. No, page number 11. My apologies. Page number 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to Mr. Praljak's Defence, I'd like to point out that on the map provided to us by Mr. Praljak, we can see two roads. Well, roads or perhaps paths.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this was the road from the top of Uzricje, and then it goes on towards Braci [phoen] and Pidris.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Maybe it should be photograph 13. I'm trying to locate the photograph, Your Honours, because it's a bit difficult with the e-court numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the document you showed a minute ago I have the number 275, a handwritten number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a hard copy here of the photograph. Maybe it would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So place it on the ELMO. It will be quicker. Place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You will have to put it on the overhead projector so that everyone can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, can you take a look at this photograph. And you said you've been referring to this route to Pidris where you saw the tanks. Can you actually see that road on this particular photograph? And you will have to -- you can also look at the photograph on the ELMO. You don't necessarily have to look at the screen. It's probably better if you look at the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, have a look at the photograph to your right, which is clearer than the one on the screen. It's difficult to make out the path on the screen. It's a lot more clearer on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Put your finger on the road so that everyone can see. Put your finger on the road.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Uzricje, and it links up with the top here. This is the road for Mracaj, Pidris, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you use your finger to point to the location at which you saw the tank.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was here. There was a field.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Would that be sufficient, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Defence had this photograph in front of them. Mr. Karnavas, you had the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. We still need to make a record in the sense that she should draw something. We saw the demonstration. Now we need to have something memorialised for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Maybe, Witness, then if you could take a pen and then indicate again with an X where you actually saw the tanks on the road.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And then maybe if we can get an IC number for this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC 69, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you then maybe put your initials and the date in the corner of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Put your initials on the document, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: All right. We'll leave the photograph for now, Witness. Witness, you said that -- that the men came out with a white flag. Did the men surrender?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It wasn't a flag. It was a big white piece of cloth. They took it out on the balcony, attached it to a pole so that they would stop shooting, so that they would understand that they wanted to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Around what happened after -- after this white -- after this white piece of cloth was shown and people surrendered? What happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The troops withdrew. The civilians were provided with assistance. I don't know how long this lasted. Then they said we had to go to Paloc. Whoever was able to go had to go there. Others would be carried there since there were people who had been seriously wounded. They didn't have any stretchers, so they wrapped them up in blankets, and then four individuals would carry these wounded persons wrapped up in blankets there. There was a doctor waiting there, there to --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... "they said that we had to go to Paloc." Who are you referring to when you say "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they told our troops -- I don't really know the details, but they said that we had to go to Paloc. Whoever could walk there had to walk there. Others were carried in blankets. Our troops ordered us to do this because we didn't see any HVO soldiers in the village then. Whoever could go there went there. There were doctors waiting there. The doctor was a Croatian doctor, and there were two medical orderlies. There were seriously wounded people who would have succumbed to their wounds if they hadn't been provided with treatment. There were two ambulances that went to Bugojno, so there was a doctor and two ambulances there. They took the wounded there, to Bugojno, if they couldn't be aided in Paloc. They even had to be operated on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, let me just stop you there. So you said that people were getting medical treatment. Are you now talking about medical treatment in Paloc or in Dusa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in Paloc. Wounds were only dressed in Dusa, but when we arrived in the house in Paloc, they were treated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, you yourself, Witness, you were also wounded. Where was your wound treated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was also wounded. They examined me there. They said they couldn't help me, that I had to go to Bugojno. I was also treated in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: How many people were -- were treated in Bugojno? Were you the only one who was taken to Bugojno, or were others taken to Bugojno as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't really provide you with any exact numbers. At that time, it wasn't possible to count. I know that the ambulance left on one occasion with two seriously wounded individuals. They then returned to fetch us and treated those who couldn't be helped by the doctors that day, treated those who had to go to Bugojno, and in Bugojno they also treated us and we then returned to Paloc.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you return to Paloc on the same day or was that the next day, or when did you return to Paloc?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I returned in the ambulance on the very same day. I returned to Paloc.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So what happened to you after you had returned to Paloc?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We stayed in Paloc for two or three days. The men were taken away immediately. We were in the house. No one came to see us. There were no guards protecting us. The women who were fit left, and they'd prepare food, and they also came to bury those who had died.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When you say, "They also came to bury those who had died," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They let them bury them and then return them to detention, to the detention units that they had been held in before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But -- so you did answer my question, Witness. You said, "They let them bury them." Now, who are "they," and who are "them"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO released our soldiers so that they could come and bury the civilians who had died. And after they had been buried, they were returned to the detention units they'd been held in. They spent some time in Paloc, then they were transferred to Trnovaca, and then some went to Prozor, and others remained in Trnovaca, and we never saw them again. After burials, we didn't see any of our soldiers again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Paloc?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we were there for between two and three days, and then we returned there. They said, "Go home." We were put up in three houses. We moved from Paloc. When we arrived there there were some troops there. We were put up in three houses and then an order of some kind was issued. We were all told to gather in one place. We were supposed to go to Hajrudin Sljivo's house. We were to assemble there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me just stop you there. So you said you returned to Dusa and you were put in three houses. Were these houses in the upper part of Dusa or in the lower part of Dusa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the lower part of Dusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And you say that there were troops there. Can you describe what kind of troops were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were troops with Croatian insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you describe how these soldiers looked like? What were they wearing, if they had patches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were wearing camouflage uniforms. They had HVO insignia on their sleeves. They were wearing jackets.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now -- so you said you were first put in three houses. What can you say about the condition of the houses in lower Dusa where you were taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it all took place within 10 or 15 minutes. We didn't stay at the houses. Then there was an order according to which we should all be placed in Hajrudin's house. So we were in those houses for 10 or 15 minutes. Then we all gathered in Hajrudin's house, in the house of Hajrudin Sljivo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And did anything particular happen when you moved from those three houses into Hajrudin Sljivo's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we went there. I don't know how many troops there were, exactly how many HVO members there were exactly. We were lined up. They had their rifles at the ready. I don't know what sort of orders they were waiting for. One soldier asked a question. We then realised that he wasn't a local inhabitant. He pointed to the villages of Odvoda [phoen] and Batusa. In Odvoda there were just Muslims, and in Batusa there were Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You said we realised that this soldier was not a local inhabitant. Why are you saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, because he didn't know about these villages that he had asked about. So it was probably the first time he had come there. All the locals know about the population structure of the various villages. They know which villages are inhabited by Muslims and which villages are inhabited by Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, how many soldiers were there? Could you provide us with an approximate number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know exactly. They -- well, we were all in a state of shock, so I couldn't really say how many of them there were. Some of them drove through in jeeps. They passed through Old Dusa, Stara Dusa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 23 [as interpreted] you said they drive through in jeeps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They had these registration plates on the jeeps. They'd pass through the village. We were in the lower part of Dusa. And they had the letters MO on the jeeps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said there was a -- there were the letters M on the jeep. Just the M or was there a number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I couldn't really see everything clearly, but when they passed through you'd notice the vehicle, but I didn't really notice the letters. I noticed those two letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But was there one jeep or several jeeps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they drove through. I couldn't count them. They went in various directions. I couldn't provide with you an exact number. Some were coming back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you see one vehicle or several?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they'd drive through and return. On one occasion two drove through and then they returned. So it was difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, please carry on. Try to accelerate so that the cross-examination can commence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just one question on the questions that were asked by the Judge. You said that the letters were -- were MO. Does that refer to a certain region and, if so, what region?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most probably -- [no interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mostar. I came to the -- to this conclusion judging by the letters I saw, MO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honours, on line 57 -- page 57, line 3, the witness actually said MO and not just -- just M.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, when you came back to Dusa, what can you say about the condition of the houses in Dusa? You said you were taken first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, because I see that my words were not interpreted. I wanted to say that the interpreters in the French booth heard the letter M, not MO. The witness confirmed that it was MO. So we take note of that. So, madam, did you see the letter M or MO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] MO. I'm not blind not to see. There was a road there and they passed along that road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, so just -- I'll ask my question again. When -- when you came back to Dusa, what was the condition of -- of the houses in Dusa? And you said you arrived in the lower part of Dusa, so maybe we can start by talking about the lower part of Dusa.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we were in Paloc, the Behlos' houses were burnt that day when we were surrendering. So Behlos' houses were burnt. And then afterwards they started torching other houses in Donja Dusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And when you've been referring to Donja Dusa. Is that Upper Dusa or Lower Dusa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's lower. It's a village lower down. It's a new settlement, and this new one was called as New Dusa, or Lower Dusa, and the older one was Old Dusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you see that these houses in Lower Dusa were being torched? Did you see that yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A neighbour who was leaving her house, we were about 20 metres away, soldiers were there, she was trying to prevent them from torching her house. They might have killed her if it hadn't been for her father-in-law who told her there was nothing she could do to prevent it. And then they set fire to her house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, again I would like you to be more specific. You're talking about soldiers and you're talking about "they." What kind of soldiers were these?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO. HVO soldiers were there. And she was coming out of the house, and they came in front of the door. I couldn't hear what they were saying, but she was trying to prevent them from setting fire to her house. And then her father-in-law said, "You can't do anything." And then they pushed her away with their rifle, and they entered and set fire to the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: How many soldiers did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three soldiers. Whether there were others behind the house -- because the houses were very close, one to another. We couldn't move around much outside. We don't know where the bullets were coming from, whether it was for intimidation. When you go out to hang the laundry, you could hear a bullet whiz over your head. So that we didn't move around much, especially not in the fields. We stayed inside as much as we could out of fear. We were afraid. But the bullets were coming from some place, though we couldn't see exactly where from, nor the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, how long did you -- did you stay in Hajrudin Sljivo's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly. I can tell you roughly. UNPROFOR came to visit us --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just give me roughly the number of days that you stayed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some 10 days or so probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just ask you this: Were you able to see the houses from the lower part of -- of Dusa? Were you able to see Upper Dusa from the house that you were in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We could see everything as they were burning. When they came, they set fire to our whole village. The whole village of Dusa. The stables, even the cows. You really don't know to say. One can only cry and watch the fire. At the end, I just laughed. And people said, "Why are you laughing?" And I said, "I can no longer cry." You could see flames. Even the older houses were burning, and stables full of hay. All the houses in Dusa were torched that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. A couple of questions on what you just said. You first said, "When they came, they set fire to our whole village." Again, who are "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. The Croatian army. A car went by without any markings. There was nothing on the vehicle. It was the same colour as the clothing they wore, and that is when everything was set fire to. It was completely destroyed and nothing was left there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A point of clarification. You said the Croatian army. You mean the HVO or the army from Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. The HVO. The HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You're describing this. Were you actually able to witness this yourself? Where were you when this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in -- in front of Hajrudin's house when the vehicle passed by and when the houses were torched. No one went up there. Nobody dared go there. Afterwards, we went there because Sljivo Enver's house was not set on fire. The second floor hadn't burned down. The first had. The second hadn't. Because there was nothing there on the second floor. There were just the walls. There were bullet holes in the door, in the frame of the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You say afterwards we went to -- to Enver Sljivo house. When was this, and with whom did you go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went there -- UNPROFOR came, and we felt safer when they came. We were happy to see that everyone hadn't forgotten us. And we went there. We entered the house. One couldn't believe what one saw. The first floor was burned. We climbed to the second floor. It wasn't burnt, but the door had bullet holes -- or, rather, each door-frame had these bullet holes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So what happened to you after -- after you left the house of Hajrudin Sljivo? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to Gornji Vakuf. UNPROFOR came to take us. We were driven to Vakuf, put up there. Then there was an exchange of soldiers, and they returned that day. Our soldiers returned. Some stayed behind. They thought they could protect their property and prevent it from being burnt if they stayed, so some of them stayed whose houses had not been burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I shall be the first, Your Honour. I assume I have 15 minutes. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Try and be brief. If everyone takes 15 minutes, we won't manage, so we should try and complete the hearing by a quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall do my best, but I'll take little longer than 15 minutes because I have permission from Mr. Pusic's counsel to use a little of their time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I have a few questions for you, but I would first like to ask you to have a look at the photograph that has already been shown you, 09146, photograph number 5. We can see here some sand. That would roughly be the spot where your house used to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Am I right if I say that the sand by shape looks like the foundations of your house? And if I understood your drawing properly, that the main entrance would be roughly across the way from this car.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, the entrance was on the other side towards me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What do you mean, in relation to the car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The entrance to the garage was across the way from the car, but the main entrance was on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You mean towards the electricity pole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. The other side. On this side.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So the side closest to us. That is where the main entrance was; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When you drew the -- where the shell hit the basement, was it the lateral part of the house towards this tree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, towards the tree.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So not on this front wall but the side wall towards the house. So could we please draw on the top of these foundations the way your house stood? Could you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll try.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please do that. On top of this sand, as you see it, could you draw your house as it used to be. I think you can use the rectangle that you see on the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Excellent. So that is where your house stood.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I think we'll need to go into private session with the exercise we're doing now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And I would request that the earlier part be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a few minutes we shall have to have a break.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I am concerned, we can have the break now if you wish, Your Honour. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many more minutes do you need? I think it would be better for you to finish first. How many more minutes do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's hard for me to say in view of the reactions of the witness. Maybe some 10 minutes or so, and my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but then we have Mr. Karnavas and Ms. Alaburic. So that's what we're worried about. Unless Mr. Karnavas wishes to give him -- give you his time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, a pause is always good for one to reflect and perhaps condense whatever is left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will have the break now. It's 25 to 1.00. We will resume at 10 to 1.00, and we will continue until a quarter to 2.00. So please try and come to understanding so that we can adjourn on time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I looked through my questions, and I personally have no further questions, but my client feels that three technical questions need to be put and that will only take five minutes. But we have reached agreement regarding the use of time, and I'm sure we will be able to adjourn on time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, madam. Let me ask you some very simple technical questions. You have drawn where the shell hit your house. You said that it entered the corridor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the corridor and the basement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: What kind of a hole did it leave; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Enormous hole, a big hole.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Was it a round hole? How big was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I say it's a big hole, you know what is a small hole and a big hole.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It was a round hole and the shell hit directly at the house. It --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The way I told you. It was an enormous hole. As the corridor leads to the basement, it landed into the basement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could we have 09149. Could we see -- have the sketch on the ELMO, please. In the meantime, can you please show us on the sketch shown by the Prosecutor the exact position where the shell fell in accordance with the sketch you drew for Mrs. Nozica. I think it is point 264, but will you please draw it yourself now. I think it would be where arrow number 264 is, according to what -- the drawing that you made before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you can see the road leading towards Uzricje, and to the left or above would you see the hill known as Mackovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mackovac and Kuk and so on, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And as far as I can remember, there are two roads on Mackovac, an upper road and a lower road. Could you please draw a circle where Mackovac is. In relation to Uzricje, it would be above Uzricje. It says Uzricje. You see the word there? According to the map I have, Mackovac is somewhere about -- it's parallel with Dusa and Uzricje. Never mind. It's not important. Where this drawing is, that is where Mackovac is. When you were pointing things out to us, could you now indicate where the tank -- tank was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am -- I am afraid I can't mark that for you. I know that the shots were coming from that side, but I really can't do that, not even approximately.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let us go slowly. You were on the balcony, and you looked towards the hill facing the front of your house. In the woods, on a road you saw a tank. So try and imagine yourself standing on that same balcony facing the hill, and up there on a road or in the woods you saw a couple of tanks. Could you roughly indicate where that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't find my way on this drawing. I think I indicated it clearly on the other drawing, but not on this one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have this reconstructed. But since you said that it made a hole and that this arrow indicates where the shell made this hole and penetrated into the basement, if you have a look through that hole can you see Mackovac, or do you see something that is opposite Gornji Vakuf? When you turn in that direction, Uzricje would be to your left.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I really can't answer that question. How can I say this? Whoever fired those shells knew how they were doing this, but the site operator must have been very good.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But do you know where the graveyard is? Have a look at the rectangular -- at the rectangle to the right of your house. Do you know where the graveyard is located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Where was the tank in relation to the graveyard? Now you know where the graveyard is. So now you could say perhaps whether it was above, to the left, to the right, in relation to the graveyard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether it was fired from that location or not, but the house was hit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Just tell us where the tank was in relation to the graveyard. Later we'll talk about the house that was hit, et cetera. But in relation to the graveyard, where was the tank located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have marked the location now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So that's where it was. Thank you. Could you just write down the word "tank."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, in order to assist you, we have a photograph where we can see the hill, the graveyard, et cetera. It might be more useful to show this photograph. The number is 273. Since we have this photograph, place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Next to the red dot on the house could you write down G.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be perhaps be easier --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you also sign the document and put down -- and note the date. Put your initials on the previous document and today's date. It's the 27th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If she signs it, maybe she can sign it with her pseudonym instead of her name since we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You should use your pseudonym, madam, BY. Not on the photograph, though, on the other document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] BY. I can't see BY.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There it is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a number for Mr. Praljak's document under seal, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honours, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, you have a photograph on the ELMO in which it seems that we can see the graveyard. We can see the graves, and in the foreground we can see what seems to be the stable, and in the background we can see the hill. Is this actually what one can see from your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, there's a photograph with the graveyard. Perhaps you could put your questions to her and use the photograph if you feel it's necessary. If not, don't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In this photograph -- well, there's a path up in the woods, but in this photograph could you mark approximately the location of the tank when you saw it on that day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the morning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In the morning. Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Should I mark this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Mark the location where the tank was. Adjust the photograph for yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a field here and the path passed through here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you please speak up. That's where you saw the tank. Madam, this position is quite different from the one that you indicated on the previous photograph, and it's quite different from the position indicated by the previous witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm telling you about what I saw. I'm not interested in any other witnesses. What I saw that morning is what I'll tell you about, but as to whether it fired from that location or from some other location, I don't know, but that morning there were two tanks on the road there. There was another road too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. There were two tanks there, and you did -- and you saw them. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, would you want to tender this document into evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, could you mark BY on this document. Write down the initials BY.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have a number for the photograph under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] IC 72, Your Honours, under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You said that at one point in time you saw one or two jeeps and the registration plate said MO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You've seen American films, and you see these American jeeps. Were they such jeeps or were they four-wheel vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's the first time I saw those jeeps. What armija didn't have the HVO had. I won't talk about films now. That's the first time I saw them. I was dumbfounded when I saw such jeeps during the war, when I noticed that they had such equipment, such vehicles.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Were these open jeeps or were they closed? Did they have roofs above them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were closed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did they have a sort of cabin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say. They passed by quickly. You didn't have time to observe them. You didn't have time to see whether there was a tarpaulin covering them or not. You didn't feel free to observe. We were lined up. There were rifles pointed at us, and these vehicles just drove by. We were by the road, lined up there, and there were the rifles there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, the -- Mr. Praljak is asking you whether the jeeps resemble jeeps one sees in American films. For example, American jeeps as used in the Second World War. Were the jeeps you saw of such kind, or were the jeeps more like Japanese all-terrain vehicles, Toyota all-terrain vehicles? So were they Japanese all-terrain vehicles or were they American-style vehicles? If you don't know, just say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. Those who sent them there know what kind of jeeps they were, but you're asking me about this and I don't know. All I know is that they drove through.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said HVO soldiers torched houses in part of Dusa, and then you said, "I saw three soldiers."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was down there. Naturally I saw them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You saw three soldiers. When? At what time of day did they pass through? Was it in the evening, in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon when the entire upper part of Dusa had been set on fire. It was in the afternoon, perhaps about 1.00 or 2.00 p.m., when Gornja Dusa burnt down.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can you tell me the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I keep saying that I can't remember the dates. I wish I could remember the dates, but none of the civilians even knew what time it was nor whether it was Monday or Friday or what the date was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. You said the car had no markings. You said that there were three soldiers in that car.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I said that there were three soldiers down there by the house, and they wanted to set fire to it. It was Sljivo Sevka's house, so there were no cars. But when Gornja Dusa was on fire then the car without any markings passed by. They went to Gornja Dusa and then everything was set fire to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, we have to stop there because we've run out of time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just clarify this issue and then I'll be finished.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: At the time they passed by, those HVO soldiers that you had previously seen there were no longer there or were they still there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the soldiers had withdrawn. The ones who had these modern jeeps, well, they had stayed there for two or three days. They no longer appeared and then ordinary jeeps started arriving. But for two or three days they were there with these real jeeps.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no more questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Witness. I have a few simple and brief questions that I would like to put to you, and I hope that we will manage to cover all the ground that I think is important. You said today a lot about how the shell fell on your house. My colleague has just drawn my attention to the fact that I have made a mistake since we're in open session. Could this please be taken into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move back into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 30th day of October, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.50 p.m.,
